report:
## Summary

The evidence is genuinely mixed, and your "no" answer is defensible but not the full consensus. Several observational studies and meta-analyses do find statistical associations between benzodiazepine/Z-drug use and later dementia diagnosis—for example, a UK Biobank-style meta-analysis found pooled OR ~1.38 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10608561/), and other cohorts report hazard ratios around 1.4–1.6 (https://www.bmj.com/content/345/bmj.e6231).

However, methodologically stronger studies suggest these associations largely reflect **confounding by indication and reverse causation** rather than a true causal effect. Anxiety, depression, and sleep disturbance—the conditions benzodiazepines treat—are themselves early symptoms/risk markers of dementia, so people who later develop dementia are more likely to have been prescribed these drugs *before* diagnosis, not because the drugs caused the disease (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26715389/). Studies designed to reduce this bias—using active-comparator/new-user designs comparing benzodiazepines to other psychiatric drugs, or excluding use in the years just before diagnosis—generally find little or no residual association (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11218055/, Healio summary of the American Journal of Psychiatry nationwide cohort study). One recent reanalysis explicitly titled "Clearing the confounding confusion" concluded only a modest dose-related signal remained after adjustment, largely attributable to confounding (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167494325001086).

**Conclusion:** Raw associations between sedative/hypnotic use and dementia exist in many studies, but the best-designed research indicates these are mostly explained by prodromal symptoms and shared risk factors rather than a causal drug effect. So "no, these drugs likely don't directly cause Alzheimer's/dementia" is a reasonable, evidence-supported position, though not unanimous—caution with long-term, high-dose use in older adults is still prudent given uncertainty and other known risks (falls, cognitive impairment, dependence).
